articles.title: Detecting Abnormal Keyed-Entry Rates from POS Entry Mode Data
articles.excerpt: Every card authorization carries a small field that records how the card data reached the terminal: chip, contactless, magnetic stripe, fallback swipe, or typed in by hand. Most engineering teams neve…
articles.body: Every card authorization carries a small field that records how the card data reached the terminal: chip, contactless, magnetic stripe, fallback swipe, or typed in by hand. Most engineering teams never look at it. They should. A terminal or cashier that keys in far more sales than its peers usually points to a broken reader, a training gap, or someone deliberately bypassing the chip. Keyed sales also cost more and are harder to defend in disputes. This article covers building a keyed-rate monitor: normalizing entry mode data, separating keyed-by-design traffic, scoring terminals and employees without drowning in small-sample noise, and triaging alerts.
articles.author: Jarrod Wright

articles.title: I saw my local shopkeeper writing things
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle So one evening i was just sitting at my local grocery store, gossiping with bhaiya like i usually do. While we w…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built So one evening i was just sitting at my local grocery store, gossiping with bhaiya like i usually do. While we were talking a customer came, bought 2 Maggi and a Parle-G and bhaiya opened this old diary and wrote it down by hand. Then another customer came. And another. Same diary, same pen. I asked him "bhaiya aapko kaise pata chalta hai kya sabse zyada bikta hai?" and he just laughed and said "andaaza hai, roz dekhta hoon toh pata chal jaata hai". No numbers, no research, just a guess. And that guess decides how much stock he buys from the wholesaler every week. If he guesses wrong his money is stuck in stuff that doesnt sell, or he runs out of the stuff that does.

articles.title: How Do You Threat-Model an Application That Uses Autonomous AI Agents?
articles.excerpt: You spent years building a threat model you trust. You know your trust boundaries, you've mapped your data flows, and your team can recite STRIDE in their sleep. Then someone shipped an autonomous AI…
articles.body: You spent years building a threat model you trust. You know your trust boundaries, you've mapped your data flows, and your team can recite STRIDE in their sleep. Then someone shipped an autonomous AI agent into the product, and quietly, every assumption underneath that model cracked. Here's the problem in one sentence: traditional software does what you programmed it to do, but an autonomous agent does what it is convinced to do. Those are not the same risk. An agent that reads customer emails, queries your database, calls third-party APIs, and writes to your file system is not a function you can fully specify. It is a decision-maker operating on untrusted input, and the input arrives in the same channel as its instructions. That last point is the whole game.
articles.author: Ben Johnson

articles.title: I finally cut AI context bloat by 80% and the fix was embarrassingly simple
articles.excerpt: A few months ago I watched an agent do something deeply cursed. It had already fetched the data. And then it pasted the entire raw tool response into the next model call anyway. Full JSON blobs. Logs.…
articles.body: A few months ago I watched an agent do something deeply cursed. It had already fetched the data. It had already parsed the data. It had already stored the useful fields. And then it pasted the entire raw tool response into the next model call anyway. Full JSON blobs. Logs. Metadata. Useless fields. Everything. The next step got slower. The step after that got more expensive. Then the model started doing that annoying thing where it answers the easy part of the task and quietly ignores the important part. That was the moment the bug became obvious: Most “context window problems” are not model problems. They are state management problems. Once you see that, you start spotting it everywhere in n8n flows, LangGraph agents, MCP tool loops, and custom OpenAI-compatible orchestration code.
articles.author: Lars Winstand

articles.title: Artificial intelligence created an attack for Chrome in six days
articles.excerpt: Researchers at security firm XBOW used an AI model to build a full-chain Google Chrome exploit combining three unknown bugs in six days. The agentic workflow handled source code analysis, proof-of-con…
articles.body: Researchers at security firm XBOW used an AI model to build a full-chain Google Chrome exploit combining three unknown bugs in six days. The agentic workflow handled source code analysis, proof-of-concept testing, and initial drafts. Google confirmed the vulnerabilities, released patches, and paid a $250,000 reward. Security firm XBOW announced that its researchers used a publicly available artificial intelligence model to connect three previously unknown Chrome vulnerabilities. The result was an attack that could execute code on a Windows computer simply by visiting a web page, without the user having to click or download anything. Google confirmed the issues, fixed them, and awarded XBOW the maximum bounty of $250.000 for a complete attack of this type.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Stitch Desk is a local-first order assistant for boutiques and tailors. Many small tailoring shops still run on…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built Stitch Desk is a local-first order assistant for boutiques and tailors. Many small tailoring shops still run on paper notebooks, loose receipts, and WhatsApp chats. A customer's measurements are in one place, the delivery date is on a sticky note, and the balance is in the owner's head. In busy seasons, that is where orders get lost and deliveries get late. Stitch Desk turns that into one small app: Note to order card: The owner types or pastes a messy note, like "Anna, bridal lehenga, boat neck blouse, deep U back, bust 36, waist 30, delivery 20 Nov, total 24000, advance 10000" .

articles.body: A "jellyfish" in the early-morning sky created by SpaceX's launch of the CRS-35 cargo mission on Oct. 13, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Did you see a gigantic, glowing jellyfish in the night sky early on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13)? If so, it's not an alien invasion (sorry); it was SpaceX launching its latest mission to the International Space Station (ISS). What is it? Just before dawn on Tuesday (Oct. 13), a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, carrying to space a robotic Dragon capsule filled with thousands of pounds of cargo. The liftoff kicked off CRS-35, the 35th mission that SpaceX is flying to the ISS as part of the company's Commercial Resupply Services agreement with NASA.

articles.excerpt: NASA's DART mission made a cosmic mess four years ago — and now a new spacecraft is ready to scout out exactly what the first-of-its-kind collision accomplished.
articles.body: NASA's DART mission made a cosmic mess four years ago — and now a new spacecraft is ready to scout out exactly what the first-of-its-kind collision accomplished. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft slammed into a small space rock called Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, in humanity's first test of planetary defense. That's the field dedicated to protecting Earth from the possibility of a calamitous asteroid impact, and DART mimicked how humans could change the orbit of a threatening space rock, taking it off its collision course. The mission definitely succeeded, shortening the little asteroid's orbit around a larger rock called Didymos by about 33 minutes .

articles.body: Now you see them, now you don't. Scientists have discovered that some of the universe's most powerful explosions, hypernovas, may not happen at all. These explosions, known as hypernovas , were first proposed to explain unusual stars in the halo of our galaxy, the Milky Way , and in a neighboring dwarf galaxy. It was suggested that these stars could only form from the debris of an explosion 10 times more powerful than the 'average' supernovas . The team behind these new findings suggests that ordinary supernovas could actually account for these stars when the uneven or non-spherical way they fling out matter is considered. "If we look at a supernova today, the star's materials are not spread evenly. Oxygen might predominantly fly in one direction, sulphur in another.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 13, 1773: Astronomer Charles Messier discovers the Whirlpool Galaxy before we ever knew it was a galaxy
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the "Whirlpool Galaxy," also known as Messier 51, or M51. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the " Whirlpool Galaxy , " also known as Messier 51, or M51. Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy. Seventy-two years later, another astronomer named William Parsons saw the whirlpool shape, but he thought it was a spiral nebula. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies. Spiral galaxy M51 (NGC 5194), The Whirlpool Galaxy, displays its long arms which consist of stars and gas laced with dust arranged in long lanes, in this view from the Hubble Space Telescope.
